title: Luxor in One Day: East & West Bank Itinerary
excerpt: Yes, you can see Luxor in one day: Karnak, Luxor Temple, the Valley of the Kings and Hatshepsut in nine hours, from €75 with tickets included. See the plan.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

Yes, you can see Luxor in one day. A planned nine-hour route covers Karnak Temple, Luxor Temple, the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens, the Colossi of Memnon and the Temple of Hatshepsut, split across the two banks of the Nile. What one day cannot fit: Medinet Habu, Deir el-Medina and the Luxor Museum. They are good reasons to stay a second night, not to rush the first.

UNESCO documents the temples and necropolis of ancient Thebes, including Luxor and its West Bank.

Most travellers arrive in Luxor with exactly one day (a Nile cruise stopover or a tight overland schedule) and a guidebook listing a dozen must-sees. The good news is that one day does cover Luxor's headline sights, if you work the geography instead of fighting it. Below: the running order of a live nine-hour tour, what it costs, what to cut, and the mistakes that quietly eat your day. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure platform, lists Luxor tours run by Ministry-licensed agencies.

Luxor in one day: what's realistic, and what gets cut

A single well-planned day covers Luxor's six headline sights: Karnak Temple, Luxor Temple, the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens, the Colossi of Memnon and the Temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari. What it cannot cover is depth: the painted workers' tombs at Deir el-Medina, the war reliefs of Medinet Habu, the Luxor Museum, and the far temples of Dendera and Abydos to the north. Ancient Thebes was Egypt's capital for much of the New Kingdom and the cult centre of Amun-Ra, and its necropolis has been UNESCO-listed since 1979. A one-day visit skips the second tier, never the first.

East Bank and West Bank: the geography that decides your route

The Nile splits Luxor in two, and the split is theological as much as geographic. The East Bank was the city of the living, with the great temples of Amun-Ra at Karnak and Luxor Temple. The West Bank, where the sun sets, became the city of the dead: royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings, mortuary temples like Hatshepsut's, and the workmen's village. Every one-day itinerary is really two half-days joined by a river crossing. Tours cross by motorboat, and the transfer takes a good half-hour or more door to door; independent travellers use the local passenger ferry, a short crossing for a small fare. The road bridge sits some distance from the sights, which makes it little use for a sightseeing day.

Cross the Nile once. The crossing (assembling, boarding, the sail and the transfer) costs the best part of an hour once everything is counted. Every extra bank switch burns most of an hour, so a one-day Luxor route should cross exactly once, in one direction, with no doubling back.

The one-day Luxor itinerary, stop by stop

This is the running order of the Luxor in Depth: East & West Bank Full Day shared departure, about nine hours with hotel pickup included (as listed in November 2026). The order can shift with traffic, site entry flow and the group's pace.

Order Where Why this slot
Start Hotel pickup, East Bank An early start keeps you ahead of the coach crowds all day.
1 Luxor Temple The quietest hour at the temple once linked to Karnak by the Avenue of Sphinxes.
2 Karnak Temple The largest religious complex of ancient Egypt: the great hypostyle hall, the obelisks, the sacred lake.
3 Nile crossing to the West Bank Motorboat crossing with the whole river in view.
4 Valley of the Kings Three royal tombs on the standard ticket; special tombs such as Tutankhamun's (KV62) are a separate ticket, not included.
5 Lunch break A break before the afternoon heat peaks; check the departure page for whether lunch is included.
6 Valley of the Queens Royal wives' and princes' tombs; Nefertari's tomb (QV66) has been closed since March 2024.
7 Colossi of Memnon A short photo stop at the giant statues of Amenhotep III.
8 Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari The terraced mortuary temple of Egypt's female pharaoh, in the softer late light.
End Back at your Luxor hotel Door to door, the day runs roughly nine hours.

The running order looks counter-intuitive, since guidebooks say reach the Valley of the Kings at opening, but it has logic. The royal tombs stay cool underground at any hour, while Karnak's open courts are comfortable in the early morning and punishing at noon. By the time the West Bank heat peaks after lunch you are below ground in the Valley of the Queens, and Hatshepsut comes in late-afternoon light.

Tombs first: the all-day West Bank alternative

If Karnak and Luxor Temple are already under your belt, or tombs are why you came, The Grand West Bank: Tombs, Temples & Deir el-Medina spends all nine hours on the west side, from €60 per person, as listed in November 2026, with hotel pickup, a licensed guide, lunch and site tickets included. Its running order: the Valley of the Kings with three tombs; the Valley of the Queens; the Colossi of Memnon; Hatshepsut; lunch; then the two sights one-day visitors always miss: Medinet Habu, Ramesses III's fortified mortuary temple, and the artisans' village of Deir el-Medina. Special tombs, including Tutankhamun's, are not included.

The deeper West Bank day suits return visitors, archaeology lovers and photographers. First-timers usually get more from the full East and West Bank route: Karnak is Karnak.

What it costs to see Luxor in one day

On a shared small-group departure with a licensed guide, transport, hotel pickup, the Nile crossing and entry tickets included, a one-day Luxor itinerary costs from €75 per person, as listed in November 2026. Tips are extra, special tombs such as Tutankhamun's are a separate ticket, and for lunch, check the departure page. Going independently is possible, but per-site tickets, a West Bank taxi and a guide add up fast for a single day. At EGP 60 to the euro (8 November 2026), the entry tickets alone for this route come to roughly EGP 2,510 (about €42) before the ferry, taxis, lunch and a guide.

Student tickets are generally half price. Valley of the Kings tickets are sold at the Visitor Centre only and a card is effectively required, so bring one. The Ministry changes prices without much notice, so check the official ticketing portal before you go.

Insider tips for a one-day Luxor visit

Six details that make or break the day:

  • Special tombs are decided at the ticket office, not the tomb gate. Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) sells as a separate ticket at the Visitor Centre, and the list of open tombs rotates. Decide before you queue.
  • The tombs are the air-conditioning. Schedule open sites such as Karnak and Hatshepsut's terraces for the shoulders of the day, and be underground from midday to mid-afternoon, when the West Bank heat peaks.
  • Luxor Temple works after dark. It stays open into the evening and is floodlit, so independent travellers can flip the plan: morning at Karnak, Luxor Temple at night.
  • Ask the guide to point out the Avenue of Sphinxes. The 2.7-kilometre processional road once linked Luxor Temple to Karnak and reopened to the public in November 2021; you pass its excavated stretches en route.
  • Baksheesh is part of the day. Baksheesh, the Egyptian custom of small tips for small services, covers toilet attendants and site helpers; guides and drivers are tipped at the day's end, separately from the tour price.
  • Balloons and an early tour start don't mix well. Luxor's sunrise balloon flights lift off before dawn on the West Bank; combine them with this itinerary and you will nap through Karnak. Pick one early-morning commitment.

Three mistakes quietly eat the day: starting late, crossing the Nile more than once, and queueing at the wrong counter for a special tomb at the hottest hour.

The verdict on seeing Luxor in one day

One day in Luxor delivers the six headline sights if you start early, cross the Nile exactly once and decide on the special tombs before you queue. Treat a second day as a bonus, not a compromise: Medinet Habu and Deir el-Medina reward it. faq.q: Is one day really enough for Luxor's main sights?
faq.a: Yes. A nine-hour route with an early start covers Karnak, Luxor Temple, the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens, the Colossi of Memnon and Hatshepsut's temple. What one day cannot fit: Medinet Habu, Deir el-Medina and the Luxor Museum. That is a reason to add a second night rather than rush the first.

faq.q: Which Luxor sights should I cut if I run out of time?
faq.a: Cut the Valley of the Queens first; the Colossi of Memnon are only a short stop. Karnak and the Valley of the Kings are the uncuttable pair. Luxor Temple is the flexible one: it stays open into the evening and is floodlit, so you can move it to the evening if the morning runs long.

faq.q: How do I get between the East Bank and the West Bank?
faq.a: Tours cross by motorboat, which takes a good half-hour or more door to door including transfers. Independent travellers use the local passenger ferry, a short crossing for a small fare. The road bridge is too far from the sights to help: plan to cross the Nile once.

faq.q: Can I see Tutankhamun's tomb on a one-day tour?
faq.a: Yes, but it is a separate ticket (EGP 700 for a foreign adult, as of November 2026) on top of the three tombs in the standard Valley of the Kings ticket. Special tombs are not included on either Sawa Luxor tour, so budget for it yourself.

faq.q: Can I do this itinerary on my own without a tour?
faq.a: Yes. Buy tickets per site, cross by the passenger ferry and hire a taxi for the West Bank loop; the geography in this post works the same. The trade-offs: no guide, no pooled costs, and heat and queues to manage yourself. Many solo travellers find a shared departure simpler for a single day.

faq.q: What happens if a Sawa Luxor date doesn't reach four travellers?
faq.a: Nothing is charged. A date needs four travellers to be confirmed (the GoAhead), and until then the seat reservation is free. A date has until 7 days before the tour to reach four; if it does not, it is cancelled, you pay nothing, and Sawa suggests another date. Once confirmed, a date is not cancelled for low numbers: a traveller who does not pay after the GoAhead is excluded and the tour still runs for the others.
